title: Deep Learning: Design Thinking and Maker Spaces (Chapter 11, Humanity Amplified)
author: Stefan Bauschard
summary: In this chapter from Humanity Amplified, Stefan Bauschard argues that design thinking deserves a place alongside debate, entrepreneurship education, and project-based learning in the standard curriculum of any school serious about preparing students for a world where machines generate answers on demand. He opens with the Embrace infant warmer: a Stanford design team challenged to build an incubator for one percent of the usual cost traveled to rural Nepal and discovered the real problem was not price but reach, since the babies who most needed warming were born far from any hospital. The breakthrough, Bauschard stresses, was not technical brilliance but structured noticing. He then strips design thinking of its consulting-industry packaging, defining it as a repeatable five-move method (empathize, define, ideate, prototype, test) for working on problems that do not arrive with instructions, and insists it is a mindset rather than a wall of sticky notes.
points: The Embrace warmer story shows that the decisive move in design thinking was structured noticing (going to the villages) rather than technical optimization of the incubator box.
Design thinking's first commandment is that you do not know what the problem is until you have watched the people who live inside it.
Bauschard defines design thinking, following Razzouk and Shute, as an analytic and creative process to experiment, prototype, gather feedback, and redesign.
The Stanford d.school / IDEO model breaks the process into five moves: empathize, define, generate, prototype, and test, then loop back and do it again.
Each move trains a muscle conventional schooling leaves slack: empathy teaches that a first read is usually wrong; definition teaches that framing a problem is itself intellectual work.
quotes: design thinking is a repeatable method for working on problems that do not arrive with instructions
the move that made everything else possible — going to the villages instead of optimizing the box — was not a feat of technical brilliance. It was a feat of structured noticing
The students had been taught a discipline whose first commandment is that you do not know what the problem is until you have watched the people who live inside it.
The definition phase teaches that framing a problem is itself intellectual work — the Embrace team’s breakthrough was a sentence, not a circuit.

empathize with the people who have the problem, define what the problem actually is, generate many possible answers, build rough versions of the promising ones, and test those versions with real users
